name: ParGeo (parallel 3D convex hull and kd-tree library)
workload: Wall-clock time to compute 3D convex hulls of synthetic and scanned point sets on 36 cores with two-way hyper-threading, ParGeo Pseudohull / divide-and-conquer versus Qhull and CGAL (the repo's own benchmark/hull3d_bench.cpp uses 10M-point in-sphere, on-sphere, in-cube and on-cube sets plus scanned models such as Armadillo, Dragon, Buddha, Thai Statue, Lucy, but only runs ParGeo's own variants).
claimed_speedup: From a search-result snippet of the ESA 2022 paper (paper not opened): fastest ParGeo convex hull up to 44.7x self-relative parallel speedup and up to 559x speedup against the best existing sequential implementation; Pseudohull up to 43.7x parallel speedup compared to Qhull and up to 5.05x over CGAL on 3-dimensional shapes. Exact paper wording and the per-dataset table were not verified.
compiler_and_flags: Repo CMakeLists.txt: C++17, -DHOMEGROWN -pthread -mcx16 -O3 -DNDEBUG -fPIC (parlaylib homegrown scheduler); compiler name and version not stated in the repo, and the paper's setup was not readable.
hardware: 36 cores with two-way hyper-threading (72 threads; repo benchmark sets maxThreads = 72); CPU model not seen because the paper was unreachable.
stars_or_usage: 54 stars; ESA 2022 paper (LIPIcs, per search results) and PPoPP 2022 poster
tradeoffs: Needs a multicore machine to win: the headline speedups come from parallelism, not from a faster sequential algorithm. Depends on the parlaylib git submodule and Google Benchmark/Google Test. Point dimension is a template parameter (2 to 7 supported for most modules); convex hull is 2D and 3D only. The README does not discuss numerical robustness or degenerate inputs, and the repo benchmark uses float points.
caveats: Numbers are from a search-result snippet only: arxiv.org, drops.dagstuhl.de, par.nsf.gov, www.cs.ucr.edu and www.cs.umd.edu were all EGRESS_BLOCKED, so benchmark_url was NOT opened and the CPU model, compiler, flags, baseline versions and point types are unknown. Tier is C under the cloud-harness rule for snippet-only evidence; a peer-reviewed ESA 2022 paper exists (B candidate, A if the paper or artifact states compiler, flags and CPU), so re-tier when paper access is available. The repo itself carries no CGAL or Qhull comparison: benchmark/*.cpp only time ParGeo's own algorithms (serial quickhull vs pseudohull, SEB variants). The README cites only the PPoPP 2022 poster and a GeoGraph paper, while the lead named ESA 2022; the ESA title match came from the search snippet. Parallel versus sequential baselines means unequal core counts; the 559x figure is against 'best existing sequential implementation', not CGAL. Last commit 2022-09-12 (over 4 years, not archived).

name: fast_gicp (FastGICP / FastVGICP / FastVGICPCuda)
workload: Registering one pair of point-cloud scans (target 17,249 points, source 17,518 points after a 0.1 m approximate voxel grid) with GICP-family methods; wall time of a single alignment and of 100 repeated alignments, with fitness score reported.
claimed_speedup: README table, i9-9900K + RTX 2080 Ti: pcl_gicp single 127.508 ms, 100 times 12549.4 ms (fitness 0.204892); pcl_ndt single 53.5904 ms, 100 times 5467.16 ms; fgicp_st (single thread) 111.324 ms / 10662.7 ms; fgicp_mt 20.1602 ms / 1585 ms (fitness 0.204412); vgicp_mt 18.1106 ms / 1381 ms; vgicp_cuda (parallel_kdtree) 15.9587 ms / 1451.85 ms; vgicp_cuda (gpu_rbf_kernel) 5.91508 ms / 590.725 ms (fitness 0.20557). Derived from page data versus pcl_gicp: fgicp_mt 6.3x (single) and 7.9x (100 runs); vgicp_mt 7.0x and 9.1x; vgicp_cuda rbf kernel 21.6x and 21.2x; single-threaded fgicp_st only 1.15x and 1.18x. README headline rates: FastGICP ~40 FPS, FastGICPSingleThread ~15 FPS, FastVGICP ~70 FPS, FastVGICPCuda ~120 FPS, NDTCuda ~500 FPS.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release (CMake default Release flags) and adds OpenMP flags; no -march option seen. Compiler name and version not stated (README says tested on Ubuntu 18.04/20.04 with CUDA 11.1).
tradeoffs: Drop-in PCL registration interface, but depends on PCL, Eigen, OpenMP, Sophus and (for CUDA) nvbio. VGICP is a voxelized approximation of GICP and the GPU rbf-kernel covariance mode is described in the source as 'extremely fast but maybe a bit inaccurate' (its fitness score 0.20557 is the worst in the table). README notes that using fewer threads than the maximum can be faster in some environments. The author's newer small_gicp (already on the known list) is stated in the README to be twice as fast as fast_gicp.
caveats: Tier would be A except that the compiler is never named and the flags come only from the CMake Release default, so it stays C (own-repo benchmark with partial methodology). Benchmark code is public (src/align.cpp) but the README shows a single scan pair and one machine. Most of the speedup comes from multithreading and GPU use against PCL's default GICP/NDT; the thread count is not stated (src/align.cpp uses omp_get_max_threads for vgicp_mt and the default for fgicp_mt) and the PCL version is not stated. Iteration and convergence settings are each class's defaults and were not verified to be identical. The ICRA 2021 VGICP paper (easychair preprint) was not opened. The README links the SMRT-AIST/fast_gicp organisation in badges and install commands, so the repo may have moved. Last commit 2025-04-24 (over 12 months).

name: iOverlay (Rust polygon boolean overlay engine)
workload: Checkerboard polygon boolean-operation test with up to 8,384,513 squares, iOverlay (Rust, multithreading feature on) versus Clipper2, as reported in the project's performance comparison page.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the project's Performance Comparison page (snippet only, page not opened): 8,384,513 squares in 33.7 s for iOverlay Rust with multithreading versus 644.3 s for Clipper2, about 19x (derived from snippet data). The repo's own README chart only reports iOverlay-internal relative times (Apple M4, 24 GB, geometric mean, i32 multithreading off = 1.00x: i16 off 0.92x, i64 off 1.30x, i16 on 0.85x, i32 on 0.86x, i64 on 1.08x).
compiler_and_flags: In-repo perf app (performance/rust_app/Cargo.toml): release profile opt-level 3, lto false, codegen-units 1; it depends on crates.io i_overlay 7.0.0. Rust toolchain version and Clipper2 build flags not seen.
hardware: Apple M4, 24 GB for the in-repo relative-time chart; hardware of the Clipper2 comparison not seen.
stars_or_usage: 211 stars; over 5 million crates.io downloads (author's claim); core of georust/geo polygon boolean operations
tradeoffs: Rust crate, so usable from C++ only through an FFI layer (the API offers a flat, FFI-friendly shape hierarchy). Integer (i16/i32/i64) and float (f32/f64) engines; the large-input gain depends on the allow_multithreading Cargo feature (rayon). Also offers slicing, clipping, offsetting and spatial predicates.
caveats: Rust only, and the numbers were NOT opened: ishape-rust.github.io is EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the 33.7 s versus 644.3 s figure comes from a WebSearch snippet and was never checked against the page, the thread count, the hardware or the Clipper2 build. The repo carries no Clipper2, geo, Boost.Geometry, CGAL or GEOS comparison: performance/rust_app benchmarks only iOverlay itself, and the README SVG shows only internal engine variants. The README says multithreading matters most for bigger data sets; its own average chart shows multithreading cutting relative time by only about 8 to 17 percent on average. OpenROAD discussion #5864 (opened, written by the iOverlay author) links the same comparison page and separately claims the sister library xOverlay is 10-20x faster than Boost.Polygon in most benchmarks except Nested Squares, but gives no hardware or compiler. Tier C under the snippet-only rule; no Boost.Geometry, CGAL or GEOS baseline evidence found.

name: rhet_RNG (xromu2jr, winner of the PRNG Battle Royale)
baseline: xoshiro256++ / xoshiro256** / xoroshiro128 variants and PCG (pcg64) among the 47 PRNGs benchmarked; std::mt19937 is not among the generators listed in the README
workload: Per the README: 47 non-cryptographic PRNGs on 9 game consoles (Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/4 Pro/5, Xbox One/One X/Series X, Stadia 1080p/4K), throughput and latency tests with at least 256 GB of random data per test, using three range-mapping methods (biased modulo, unbiased masking with discard, Lemire fixed-point fastrange) over ranges 2 to 2^16.
claimed_speedup: No benchmark numbers appear in the repo. The README states that Romu2jr (RomuDuoJr with a NASAM-based seeding wrapper, xromu2jr.h) wins overall for game development, that the fixed-point (Lemire) range mapping beats biased modulo and unbiased masking, and that results are charts of relative speed per console (for example '2.2 implies the test was 2.2 faster than the slowest test that ran in this game console'). The charts themselves are images that are not in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: README: all tests built with 'top tier configuration presets' using the latest platform SDKs and Visual Studio 2019; exact flags unstated.
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; the original rhet.dev blog post is widely cited in PRNG discussions (not verified here)
tradeoffs: RomuDuoJr has a 128-bit state and no guaranteed minimum period, so some seeds can end in short cycles; the README mitigates this with a NASAM-based initializer and brute-force checks (no cycles for 32-bit seeds within 2^24 bytes, 16-bit seeds within 2^36 bytes) but it is not a proof. Chaotic generators give low-quality first outputs unless seeded through a mixer. The README charts report some PractRand failures, and the author himself suggests xoshiro256++ or sfc64 when a guaranteed period matters. The header uses reinterpret_cast type punning in as<>() and either __uint128_t or __umulh for 64-bit ranges.
caveats: Tier D: the repo is an archive of a single 2.8 KB header (xromu2jr.h) plus a copy of the 2020 blog text; there are no benchmark numbers, charts or code in it, and the author says the benchmark code is kept private for console NDA reasons, so nothing is reproducible. The rhet.dev post and the Wayback copy were not fetched (blocked hosts). Licensing: the header says the wrapper is released into the public domain by its author, there is no LICENSE file in the repo, and the Romu algorithm by Mark Overton is not covered by that statement, so usability is marked mixed (no patent grant implied). The repo owner appears to be a different account from the original author (README says the header was created by RomuDuoJr at rhet.dev). Relative results are per console and mix PRNG quality and worst-case criteria chosen by the author; the 'winner' conclusion is his weighting.

name: cauldron random.h (ziggurat normal distribution)
baseline: std::normal_distribution (driven by std::minstd_rand in the benchmark's cpp11random entry)
workload: Generating 1,000,000 standard-normal float or double samples per trial (minimum over 10 trials) in miloyip/normaldist-benchmark, camel-cdr's 128-block ziggurat with a single condensed lookup table and an LCG as the uniform source versus the benchmark's other implementations.
claimed_speedup: Issue #3 in miloyip/normaldist-benchmark (author camel-cdr), ns per sample, float: ziggurat_new 4.018, cpp11random (std::normal_distribution) 8.852, existing ziggurat 7.289, marsagliapolar 6.133, inverse 6.017, boxmuller 7.484; double: ziggurat_new 4.081, cpp11random 17.009, existing ziggurat 7.817, marsagliapolar 8.711, inverse 7.222, boxmuller 16.546. Derived from page data: 2.2x faster than std::normal_distribution for float and 4.2x for double; 1.8x and 1.9x faster than the benchmark's existing ziggurat. The issue says its implementation is 60% faster than the existing ziggurat.
tradeoffs: Single-file C header (usable from C++) with the ziggurat entry points dist_normalf_zig and dist_normal_zig that need an init call and a lookup table (128 entries, float or double) and a caller-supplied RNG function; the slow path uses log and exp. The library also offers a lower-accuracy dist_normalf_fast that was not part of this evidence. Output quality of the issue's code was not verified here (the benchmark harness has a correctness check, but the issue does not report its result).
caveats: First-party claim in a GitHub issue comment with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so tier C. The std::normal_distribution baseline is driven by std::minstd_rand, not std::mt19937, and the standard library implementation is not stated; the ziggurat uses a cheap LCG, so the gap partly reflects RNG cost (the benchmark's null entry is about 1.05 ns). The code in the issue is the author's proposed template, not literally the current cauldron function: random.h's dist_normal(f)_zig is described as based on Doorki's implementation with the same one-table idea and later changes, so the link is by author and design, not identical code. The double version builds a 64-bit value from two 32-bit LCG outputs per the issue. The cauldron repo has tools/random/bench.c (dist_normal versus dist_normal_zig, PRNGs) but publishes no results. Issue dated 2020-12-19; last repo commit 2025-02-01. The lead's '4.0 ns versus 7.3-7.8 ns' compares against the benchmark's existing ziggurat, while the std::normal_distribution figures are 8.9 ns and 17.0 ns.

name: ROOT RanluxppEngine (portable RANLUX++)
baseline: ROOT TRandom1 (RANLUX); ROOT TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) is faster than RANLUX++ in the same benchmark
workload: Average time per generated random double from a Google Benchmark microbenchmark (BM_Rndm calling Rndm() once per iteration, rootbench TRandomBenchmarks.cxx) for TRandom1, TRandom3, TRandomMixMax and TRandomRanluxpp, 10 repetitions with standard deviation under 1 percent.
claimed_speedup: ROOT blog 'Implementing and tuning RANLUX++ for ROOT' (2020-11-30): initial portable version about 30 ns per double, Sibidanov's assembly version about 8 ns, TRandom1 (RANLUX, single precision) about 62 ns, after tuning about 9 ns per number ('very close to the assembly version'), slightly slower than TRandom3 at about 3 ns. Derived from page data: about 6.9x faster than TRandom1 (62 ns versus 9 ns); 2x faster than TRandom1 already at the untuned 30 ns. Tuning gains reported: loop unrolling up to 30 percent, overflow handling up to 15 percent, native __int128 multiplication over 40 percent, carry propagation over 20 percent on GCC 7.5.0.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.1 (default); graph also covers Clang 9.0.1 and GCC 7.5.0 built from source; optimisation flags not stated in the post.
hardware: Single core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900, CentOS 8.2.2004
stars_or_usage: ROOT: 3.3k stars; used across high-energy physics; RANLUX++ shipped in ROOT 6.24
tradeoffs: Portable C++ (uses unsigned __int128 where available, with unrolling pragmas) instead of Sibidanov's x86 assembly; 576-bit LCG state stored as 9 x 64-bit words, and the generator advances in blocks via a multiply and modulo. It gives 48 random bits per double and passes TestU01 per the blog, but it is about 3x slower than ROOT's Mersenne Twister and the code sits inside ROOT (mathcore) with ROOT dependencies (TRandomEngine base class), so extracting it needs the src/ranluxpp helper headers. Provides RanluxppEngine24 and RanluxppEngine2048 plus compatibility engines for James/Luescher RANLUX.
caveats: The benchmark compares against TRandom1 (original RANLUX) and does not beat std::mt19937, PCG or xoshiro: in the same post TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) is about 3x faster. TRandom1 yields only 24-bit single-precision numbers while RANLUX++ yields 48-52 bits per double, so the work per number differs. The measured code predates correctness changes in June 2021 (commits 'Ensure full modulo operation in mod_m', 'Convert LCG state to RANLUX numbers', 'Extract only 48 bits per number', per the file history page; the blog says 52 bits per double), so the 9 ns figure was not re-measured for the shipped implementation and the tier is capped at C. Optimisation flags are not stated; the benchmark source is public (root-project/rootbench PR #200, merged 2020-12-15, 23-line file) but no results are checked in. The repo has no benchmark results for the component. The last commit shown for RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx was 2021-06-23, so the component is stable; last_commit above is the overall ROOT repo (large project, judged only for math/mathcore RanluxppEngine*).
